claim: METTL3 was upregulated in breast cancer patient tumor tissues compared to non-tumor tissues.
source: We obtained breast cancer patient tumor tissues and found that METTL3 was upregulated in tumor samples (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from paired breast cancer patient tissues shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Two short bands of METTL3 were elevated synchronously with the full-length METTL3 in breast cancer tumor samples.
source: Notably, we observed two short bands, which were all elevated synchronously with the full-length (FL) of METTL3.
evidence: Observed in immunoblot analysis of breast cancer patient tumor tissues.

claim: The two short bands of METTL3 are derived from METTL3 protein.
source: To determine whether these bands were derived from METTL3, we constructed METTL3 knockdown in human T47D breast cancer cell lines by METTL3 shRNA and found that the amount of these two short bands was abolished (Figure 1b).
evidence: Knockdown of METTL3 abolished the short bands, and reconstitution rescued their expression.

claim: Reconstitution of exogenous METTL3 in METTL3 knockdown cells rescued the expression levels of the two short bands.
source: Reconstitution of exogenous METTL3 by no tagged pMSCV-METTL3 construct in these cells rescued the expression levels of these two bands (Figure 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot analysis after reconstitution experiment.

claim: The two short forms of METTL3 are derived from the C-terminal of METTL3.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the two short bands were recognized by antibody against the C-terminal, but not N-terminal of METTL3 (Figure 1b), suggesting that these short forms are derived from the C-terminal of METTL3.
evidence: Antibody recognition pattern shows C-terminal but not N-terminal epitopes are present.

claim: The short forms of METTL3 are designated as METTL3a and METTL3b.
source: These results indicate that these short bands are METTL3 C-terminal short forms, and we designated these two short forms as METTL3a and METTL3b as indicated in the figures.
evidence: Authors' designation based on their characterization data.

claim: The short forms of METTL3 are ubiquitously expressed across multiple cell lines.
source: Further, we also observed these short bands in other cell lines, including lung cancer cell lines, renal cancer cell lines, HCT116, and MEF (mouse embryonic fibroblast) cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that these short forms may be ubiquitously expressed.
evidence: Observed in multiple different cell types including lung cancer, renal cancer, HCT116, and MEF cells.

claim: The short forms of METTL3 are generated from post-translational regulation.
source: Since both endogenous and exogenous METTL3 expression in cells could generate METTL3a and METTL3b, we hypothesized that they are most likely generated from post-translational regulation.
evidence: Both endogenous and exogenous METTL3 generate the short forms, suggesting post-translational mechanism.

claim: Purified recombinant METTL3 protein can generate the short forms when incubated with T47D cell lysates.
source: To test this possibility, we purified recombinant protein of METTL3 and incubated it with T47D cell lysates, and found that the purified METTL3-His could generate these short forms upon incubation with T47D cell lysates (Figure 1e).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assay demonstrates post-translational processing.

claim: The short forms of METTL3 are derived from post-translational products of METTL3.
source: This result indicates that these short forms are derived from post-translational products of METTL3.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro cleavage assay with purified protein.

claim: METTL3a comprises residues 239–580 of METTL3.
source: The sequencing results showed that the METTL3a N-terminal sequence was 239SKKVS243, while that of METTL3b was 197GLNSS201, revealing that residues 239–580 and 197–580 comprise METTL3a and METTL3b, respectively (Figure 1f).
evidence: Determined by Edman sequencing of purified protein bands.

claim: METTL3b comprises residues 197–580 of METTL3.
source: The sequencing results showed that the METTL3a N-terminal sequence was 239SKKVS243, while that of METTL3b was 197GLNSS201, revealing that residues 239–580 and 197–580 comprise METTL3a and METTL3b, respectively (Figure 1f).
evidence: Determined by Edman sequencing of purified protein bands.

claim: Deletion of METTL3 Q238 significantly reduces the expression of METTL3a.
source: We next generated point mutations or deletions in those conserved terminal residues, which further revealed that deletion of METTL3 Q238 (Δ238) or Q239 (Δ239) could most significantly reduce the expression of METTL3a in 293T cells (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: Mutagenesis experiments show deletion of Q238 reduces METTL3a expression.

claim: Deletion of METTL3 L198 significantly reduces the expression of METTL3b.
source: Similarly, deletion of L198 (Δ198) or L199 (Δ199) resulted in the strongest suppression of METTL3b expression (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: Mutagenesis experiments show deletion of L198 reduces METTL3b expression.

claim: Endogenous deletion of either L198 or Q238 by CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in leads to decreased expression of both short forms.
source: Notably, endogenous deletion of either L198 or Q238 (METTL3-Δ238 or METTL3-Δ198) by CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in (KI) could lead to decreased expression of both short forms (Figure 2e, f).
evidence: CRISPR knock-in experiments demonstrate requirement of these residues for short form generation.

claim: METTL3-WT, but not METTL3-Δ238, METTL3-Δ198, or METTL3-(Δ198+Δ238), can generate the short forms in vitro.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed these post-translationally generated short forms by incubation of purified recombinant METTL3 with cell lysates of T47D, and found that METTL3-WT-His, but not METTL3-Δ238-His, METTL3-Δ198-His, or METTL3-(Δ198+Δ238)-His, could generate these short forms (Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assays with mutant proteins demonstrate requirement of specific residues.

claim: METTL3a and METTL3b are post-translationally generated through highly conserved residues.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that METTL3a and METTL3b are post-translationally generated through the highly conserved residues.
evidence: Conclusion based on mutagenesis and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: METTL3a, METTL3b, METTL3-Δ198, and METTL3-Δ238 are mainly localized to the nucleus, similar to METTL3 WT.
source: Through immunofluorescence assays, we found that METTL3a, METTL3b, METTL3-Δ198, and METTL3-Δ238 were mainly localized to nucleus, similar to METTL3 WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy shows nuclear localization.

claim: METTL3a, METTL3b, METTL3-Δ198, and METTL3-Δ238 show m6A methyltransferase activity in vitro similar to METTL3-WT.
source: And, in vitro methylation assays showed that METTL3a, METTL3b, METTL3-Δ198, and METTL3-Δ238, similar to METTL3-WT, showed m6A methyltransferase activity (Figure 2h–j).
evidence: In vitro methyltransferase assays demonstrate catalytic activity.

claim: METTL3 variants have no effect on METTL3 localization or in vitro m6A methyltransferase activity.
source: These data suggest that these METTL3 variants have no effect on METTL3 localization or in vitro m6A methyltransferase activity.
evidence: Conclusion based on immunofluorescence and in vitro methyltransferase assays.

claim: Point mutations in M156 and M157 residues to alanines (2MA) lead to disappearance of METTL3c.
source: We thus performed domain mapping for METTL3 with various mutations as indicated to identify conserved residues responsible for the expression of METTL3c, and finally found that point mutations in the M156 and M157 residues to convert these highly conserved amino acids into alanines (2MA) could lead to disappearance of METTL3c (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c–g).
evidence: Mutagenesis experiments show 2MA mutation eliminates METTL3c.

claim: METTL3-2MA functions similarly to METTL3-WT in m6A dot blots and tumor cell growth assays.
source: Since METTL3c was largely absent within endogenous METTL3, combined with data from m6A dot blots and tumor cell growth assays showing that METTL3-2MA functioned similarly to METTL3-WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2h–l), we did not investigate METTL3c in the following study.
evidence: Functional assays show METTL3-2MA behaves like wild-type.

claim: Reconstitution with METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not METTL3-Δ238, METTL3a, or METTL3b, can rescue defects in cell proliferation caused by METTL3 KO in T47D cells.
source: Cell proliferation assays showed that reconstitution with METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not METTL3-Δ238, METTL3a, or METTL3b, could rescue the defects in cell proliferation caused by METTL3 KO in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines (Figure 3b, d).
evidence: Cell proliferation assays demonstrate differential rescue capacity of METTL3 variants.

claim: Reconstitution with METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not METTL3-Δ238, METTL3a, or METTL3b, can rescue defects in cell proliferation caused by METTL3 KO in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Cell proliferation assays showed that reconstitution with METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not METTL3-Δ238, METTL3a, or METTL3b, could rescue the defects in cell proliferation caused by METTL3 KO in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines (Figure 3b, d).
evidence: Cell proliferation assays demonstrate differential rescue capacity of METTL3 variants.

claim: The short form METTL3a and full-length METTL3 are both required for tumor cell proliferation.
source: These findings suggest that the short form METTL3a and FL of METTL3 are required for tumor cell proliferation, since depletion of either one of them failed to rescue the cell growth defect caused by METTL3 KO.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments showing both forms are necessary.

claim: METTL3-Δ238 KI 293T cells display decreased cell proliferation compared to METTL3 WT cells.
source: In line with these results, METTL3-Δ238 KI 293T cells displayed decrease in cell proliferation compared to METTL3 WT cells (Figure 3e, f), and reconstitution of METTL3a, but not METTL3b, could rescue the reduced cell proliferation (Figure 3g, h).
evidence: Cell proliferation assays in CRISPR knock-in cells demonstrate requirement for METTL3a.

claim: Reconstitution of METTL3a, but not METTL3b, can rescue the reduced cell proliferation in METTL3-Δ238 KI 293T cells.
source: In line with these results, METTL3-Δ238 KI 293T cells displayed decrease in cell proliferation compared to METTL3 WT cells (Figure 3e, f), and reconstitution of METTL3a, but not METTL3b, could rescue the reduced cell proliferation (Figure 3g, h).
evidence: Rescue experiments show METTL3a specifically restores proliferation.

claim: METTL3a is required for METTL3-mediated regulation of cell proliferation.
source: These data suggest that METTL3a is required for METTL3-mediated regulation of cell proliferation.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple cell proliferation rescue experiments.

claim: Reconstitution of METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 can rescue METTL3 KO-mediated defect in tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
source: Consistent with our in vitro results, we observed that reconstitution of either METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 could rescue the METTL3 KO-mediated defect in tumor growth, while expression of METTL3-Δ238 could not (Figure 3i–k).
evidence: Mouse xenograft experiments demonstrate in vivo requirement for METTL3a.

claim: Expression of METTL3-Δ238 cannot rescue METTL3 KO-mediated defect in tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
source: Consistent with our in vitro results, we observed that reconstitution of either METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 could rescue the METTL3 KO-mediated defect in tumor growth, while expression of METTL3-Δ238 could not (Figure 3i–k).
evidence: Mouse xenograft experiments demonstrate in vivo requirement for METTL3a.

claim: METTL3a is essential for METTL3-mediated regulation of breast cancer progression.
source: These results suggest that METTL3a is essential for METTL3-mediated regulation of breast cancer progression.
evidence: Conclusion based on in vivo tumor growth experiments.

claim: METTL3-mediated tumor cell growth relies on MTC for its methyltransferase activity.
source: METTL3-mediated tumor cell growth is known to rely on MTC for its methyltransferase activity (Lan et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Lan et al., 2019).

claim: METTL3-Δ238 has much weaker interaction with WTAP but retains its interaction with METTL14.
source: To this end, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP) assays in T47D and 293T cell lines and observed that METTL3-Δ238 had much weaker interaction with WTAP, but retained its interaction with METTL14, whereas METTL3-Δ198 could interact with both WTAP and METTL14 (Figure 4a, b), consistent with the phenotypic study showing that METTL3-Δ238, but not METTL3-Δ198, affected tumor cell proliferation.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate differential binding of METTL3 variants.

claim: METTL3-Δ198 can interact with both WTAP and METTL14.
source: To this end, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP) assays in T47D and 293T cell lines and observed that METTL3-Δ238 had much weaker interaction with WTAP, but retained its interaction with METTL14, whereas METTL3-Δ198 could interact with both WTAP and METTL14 (Figure 4a, b), consistent with the phenotypic study showing that METTL3-Δ238, but not METTL3-Δ198, affected tumor cell proliferation.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate differential binding of METTL3 variants.

claim: WTAP interacts with the METTL3 N-terminal leader helix domain (LH, 1–34aa).
source: Previous reports have shown that WTAP interacts with the METTL3 N-terminal leader helix domain (LH, 1–34aa), and that METTL14 can heterodimerize with METTL3 through their individual C-terminal methyltransferase domains (Schöller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Schöller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).

claim: METTL14 can heterodimerize with METTL3 through their individual C-terminal methyltransferase domains.
source: Previous reports have shown that WTAP interacts with the METTL3 N-terminal leader helix domain (LH, 1–34aa), and that METTL14 can heterodimerize with METTL3 through their individual C-terminal methyltransferase domains (Schöller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Schöller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).

claim: Both METTL3a and METTL3b fail to interact with WTAP but can bind with METTL14.
source: In line with these findings, our results showed that both METTL3a and METTL3b, which lack the METTL3 N-terminal domain, failed to interact with WTAP, but could bind with METTL14 (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show binding patterns of short forms.

claim: Reconstitution with exogenous METTL3a can rescue the decreased interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and WTAP.
source: IP assays in METTL3 knockdown (KD) 293T cells further confirmed the decreased interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and WTAP, and reconstitution with exogenous METTL3a could rescue their interaction (Figure 4c, d), indicating that METTL3a is required for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Rescue experiments demonstrate METTL3a restores METTL3-WTAP binding.

claim: METTL3a is required for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
source: IP assays in METTL3 knockdown (KD) 293T cells further confirmed the decreased interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and WTAP, and reconstitution with exogenous METTL3a could rescue their interaction (Figure 4c, d), indicating that METTL3a is required for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments with METTL3a.

claim: METTL3 is capable of self-interaction and undergoes phase separation in nuclei.
source: Recent study has shown that METTL3 is capable of self-interaction and undergoes phase separation in nuclei (Han et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Han et al., 2022).

claim: The METTL3–METTL3 interaction can occur in both 293T cell line and in vitro recombinant protein purification–IP systems.
source: Consistently, we also found that the METTL3–METTL3 interaction could occur in both 293T cell line and in vitro recombinant protein purification–IP systems (Figure 5a, b).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro binding assays demonstrate METTL3 self-interaction.

claim: The METTL3–METTL3 interaction is independent of DNA or RNA.
source: And, the METTL3–METTL3 interaction is independent of DNA or RNA (Figure 5c).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation with RNase or DNase treatment shows interaction persists.

claim: The METTL3–METTL3 interaction occurs through its C-terminal domain.
source: We further constructed METTL3 N-terminal (1–238) and C-terminal (239–580) truncation plasmids. And, IP assays showed that the METTL3–METTL3 interaction was through its C-terminal domain (Figure 5d, e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–c; Su et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2022).
evidence: Domain mapping experiments identify C-terminal region as responsible for self-interaction.

claim: The interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and METTL3-Δ238 is barely detectable but restored under exogenous expression of METTL3a.
source: Indeed, we found that the interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and METTL3-Δ238 was barely detectable, but restored under exogenous expression of METTL3a, as was its interaction with WTAP (Figure 5f), suggesting that METTL3a is required for the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, that is a prerequisite step for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show METTL3a restores self-interaction and WTAP binding.

claim: METTL3a is required for the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, which is a prerequisite step for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
source: Indeed, we found that the interaction between METTL3-Δ238 and METTL3-Δ238 was barely detectable, but restored under exogenous expression of METTL3a, as was its interaction with WTAP (Figure 5f), suggesting that METTL3a is required for the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, that is a prerequisite step for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Conclusion based on rescue experiments showing sequential requirement.

claim: WTAP only interacts with METTL3 in dense phase, which is formed by METTL3–METTL3 interaction.
source: Our finding is in line with previous study showing that WTAP only interacts with METTL3 in dense phase, which is formed by METTL3–METTL3 interaction (Han et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Han et al., 2022) and consistent with current findings.

claim: METTL3b has no effect on the METTL3–METTL3 interaction.
source: While METTL3b has no effect on the METTL3–METTL3 interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), which is consistent with our above data showing that METTL3b is dispensable for the METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show METTL3b does not affect self-interaction.

claim: METTL3 depletion decreases the METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions.
source: Through Co-IP assays with 293T cells, we found that METTL3 depletion decreased the METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions (Figure 5g), suggesting that the intracellular METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions take place at least partially through METTL3.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show METTL3 depletion affects METTL14 interactions.

claim: The intracellular METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions take place at least partially through METTL3.
source: Through Co-IP assays with 293T cells, we found that METTL3 depletion decreased the METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions (Figure 5g), suggesting that the intracellular METTL14–METTL14 and METTL14–WTAP interactions take place at least partially through METTL3.
evidence: Conclusion based on depletion experiments showing METTL3 dependency.

claim: METTL14 depletion increases the METTL3–METTL3 and METTL3–WTAP interactions.
source: While METTL14 depletion did not reduce, but rather increase the METTL3–METTL3 and METTL3–WTAP interactions (Figure 5h).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show METTL14 depletion enhances METTL3 interactions.

claim: WTAP can form dimers.
source: Recent cryo-EM data demonstrate that WTAP can form dimer (Su et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous cryo-EM structural study (Su et al., 2022).

claim: The WTAP–WTAP interaction is unaffected by depletion of METTL3.
source: As expected, we observed the WTAP–WTAP interaction in 293T cells, and it was unaffected by depletion of METTL3 (Figure 5i).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show WTAP self-interaction persists without METTL3.

claim: WTAP depletion has no effect on the METTL3–METTL3 and METTL3–METTL14 interactions.
source: Conversely, WTAP depletion had no effect on the METTL3–METTL3 and METTL3–METTL14 interactions (Figure 5j, k).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show METTL3 interactions are independent of WTAP.

claim: The METTL3–METTL3 interaction acts as a core initiating the formation of METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex.
source: Altogether, we conclude that the METTL3–METTL3 interaction acts as a core initiating the formation of METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple depletion and interaction experiments.

claim: METTL3a mediates the METTL3–METTL3 interactions, thereby forming larger complexes for efficient recruitment of WTAP in MTC.
source: These data demonstrate that METTL3a mediates the METTL3–METTL3 interactions, thereby forming larger complexes for efficient recruitment of WTAP in MTC.
evidence: Conclusion based on interaction and rescue experiments.

claim: WTAP is essential for m6A deposition.
source: WTAP is essential for m6A deposition (Liu et al., 2014; Ping et al., 2014), our current data suggest that METTL3a is required for METTL3–WTAP interaction.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Liu et al., 2014; Ping et al., 2014).

claim: Reconstitution of METTL3-Δ238 cannot rescue the decreased RNA m6A modification caused by METTL3 depletion in 293T cells.
source: Through m6A dot blot assays, we observed that reconstitution of METTL3-Δ238 could not rescue the decreased RNA m6A modification caused by METTL3 depletion in 293T cells, while reconstitution of METTL3-Δ198 or METTL3-WT in these cells restored the m6A deposition (Figure 5l, m).
evidence: m6A dot blot assays demonstrate differential rescue capacity of METTL3 variants.

claim: Reconstitution of METTL3-Δ198 or METTL3-WT restores m6A deposition in METTL3-depleted 293T cells.
source: Through m6A dot blot assays, we observed that reconstitution of METTL3-Δ238 could not rescue the decreased RNA m6A modification caused by METTL3 depletion in 293T cells, while reconstitution of METTL3-Δ198 or METTL3-WT in these cells restored the m6A deposition (Figure 5l, m).
evidence: m6A dot blot assays demonstrate differential rescue capacity of METTL3 variants.

claim: METTL3-Δ238 KI cells show reduced m6A level compared to METTL3-WT cells.
source: Consistently, METTL3-Δ238 KI cells showed reduced m6A level compared to METTL3-WT cells, and reconstitution of exogenous METTL3a in METTL3-Δ238 KI cells rescued this decrease (Figure 5n, o).
evidence: m6A dot blot assays in CRISPR knock-in cells demonstrate requirement for METTL3a.

claim: Reconstitution of exogenous METTL3a in METTL3-Δ238 KI cells rescues the decreased m6A level.
source: Consistently, METTL3-Δ238 KI cells showed reduced m6A level compared to METTL3-WT cells, and reconstitution of exogenous METTL3a in METTL3-Δ238 KI cells rescued this decrease (Figure 5n, o).
evidence: m6A dot blot assays demonstrate METTL3a restores m6A levels.

claim: METTL3a is required for the formation of METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex and m6A RNA modification.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that METTL3a is required for the formation of METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex and m6A RNA modification.
evidence: Conclusion based on interaction and m6A modification assays.

claim: m6A methylation is globally decreased in METTL3 KO cells expressing empty vector or METTL3-Δ238.
source: Mapping of transcripts with m6A modification revealed that m6A methylation was globally decreased from the transcriptome of METTL3 KO cells expressing empty vector (Vec) or METTL3-Δ238, while the total number of methylation marks was similar among METTL3-Δ198-, METTL3-WT-expressing METTL3 KO cells and the control (sgCtrl+Vec) cells (Figure 6a).
evidence: m6A-seq data shows global reduction in m6A peaks.

claim: The total number of m6A methylation marks is similar among METTL3-Δ198-, METTL3-WT-expressing METTL3 KO cells and the control cells.
source: Mapping of transcripts with m6A modification revealed that m6A methylation was globally decreased from the transcriptome of METTL3 KO cells expressing empty vector (Vec) or METTL3-Δ238, while the total number of methylation marks was similar among METTL3-Δ198-, METTL3-WT-expressing METTL3 KO cells and the control (sgCtrl+Vec) cells (Figure 6a).
evidence: m6A-seq data shows comparable m6A peak numbers.

claim: The most enriched motif of m6A-modified transcripts across all groups is the canonical GGAC motif.
source: Whereas motif analyses of the m6A peaks showed that the most enriched motif of the transcripts across all groups was the canonical GGAC motif (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), and also the distribution of m6A methylation sites across the full transcriptome were similar among all groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Motif analysis of m6A-seq data identifies consensus sequence.

claim: The distribution of m6A methylation sites across the full transcriptome is similar among all groups.
source: Whereas motif analyses of the m6A peaks showed that the most enriched motif of the transcripts across all groups was the canonical GGAC motif (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), and also the distribution of m6A methylation sites across the full transcriptome were similar among all groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: m6A-seq data shows similar distribution patterns across transcript regions.

claim: METTL3 KO cells expressing either METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 share most of their m6A peaks (>80%).
source: To identify their differentially regulated m6A methylation sites, we first normalized their m6A peaks with that of METTL3 KO cells expressing vector (sgMETTL3+Vec) to eliminate those peaks not affected by METTL3 KO, we then found that METTL3 KO cells expressing either METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 shared the most of their m6A peaks (>80%), while those cells expressing METTL3-Δ238 lost 90% of peaks observed in METTL3-WT (Figure 6b).
evidence: Comparative analysis of m6A-seq data shows overlap between METTL3-WT and METTL3-Δ198.

claim: METTL3 KO cells expressing METTL3-Δ238 lost 90% of m6A peaks observed in METTL3-WT.
source: To identify their differentially regulated m6A methylation sites, we first normalized their m6A peaks with that of METTL3 KO cells expressing vector (sgMETTL3+Vec) to eliminate those peaks not affected by METTL3 KO, we then found that METTL3 KO cells expressing either METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198 shared the most of their m6A peaks (>80%), while those cells expressing METTL3-Δ238 lost 90% of peaks observed in METTL3-WT (Figure 6b).
evidence: Comparative analysis of m6A-seq data shows dramatic loss in METTL3-Δ238.

claim: Downregulation of METTL3a inhibits the METTL3-mediated m6A deposition.
source: These analyses suggest that downregulation of METTL3a inhibits the METTL3-mediated m6A deposition.
evidence: Conclusion based on m6A-seq analysis showing global reduction.

claim: Differentially m6A-methylated gene transcripts between METTL3-WT and METTL3-Δ238 are most highly enriched in the mTOR pathway.
source: To explore the potential targets regulated by METTL3a, we analyzed mRNAs associated with differentially regulated m6A peaks in METTL3-WT- versus METTL3-Δ238-complemented METTL3 KO cells and found that the differentially modified gene transcripts were enriched in several signal transduction pathways, and most highly in the mTOR pathway (Figure 6c).
evidence: GSEA analysis of m6A-seq data identifies mTOR pathway enrichment.

claim: METTL3 promotes mTOR activity.
source: Previous studies have found that METTL3 promotes mTOR activity (Chen et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020a), although the underlying mechanism has remained unclear.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Chen et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020a).

claim: TMEM127 is significantly upregulated in METTL3 KO T47D cells.
source: Immunoblot analysis of those well-established regulators for mTOR activation showed that TMEM127, a suppressor of mTOR (Qin et al., 2010), was significantly upregulated in METTL3 KO T47D cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows increased TMEM127 protein levels upon METTL3 KO.

claim: TMEM127 is a suppressor of mTOR.
source: Immunoblot analysis of those well-established regulators for mTOR activation showed that TMEM127, a suppressor of mTOR (Qin et al., 2010), was significantly upregulated in METTL3 KO T47D cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Qin et al., 2010).

claim: METTL3 KO leads to a significant decrease in m6A peaks at the 3′UTR of TMEM127 transcript.
source: From m6A sequencing data, we observed that METTL3 KO led to a significant decrease in m6A peaks at the 3′UTR of TMEM127 transcript compared to that in cells reconstituted with METTL3-WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not METTL3-Δ238 (Figure 6f), which was further verified by m6A RIP assays in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines (Figure 6g and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: m6A-seq and m6A-RIP data show reduced m6A modification on TMEM127 transcript.

claim: METTL3-WT, but not METTL3-Δ238, can rescue TMEM127 expression in METTL3 KO T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines.
source: Subsequent immunoblot assays showed that TMEM127 was negatively regulated by METTL3, and a similar trend with the m6A-seq data was also observed that METTL3-WT, but not METTL3-Δ238 expression could rescue TMEM127 expression in METTL3 KO T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines (Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows differential rescue of TMEM127 levels by METTL3 variants.

claim: METTL3 KO-mediated decrease in S6K phosphorylation can be rescued by METTL3 WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not by METTL3-Δ238.
source: Accordingly, METTL3 KO-mediated decrease in S6K phosphorylation could be rescued by METTL3 WT or METTL3-Δ198, but not by METTL3-Δ238 (Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows differential rescue of mTOR signaling by METTL3 variants.

claim: Knockdown of TMEM127 in METTL3-depleted T47D cells restores S6K phosphorylation and cell proliferation.
source: And, knockdown of TMEM127 in the METTL3 depleted T47D cells could restore S6K phosphorylation and cell proliferation (Figure 6i, j).
evidence: Rescue experiments show TMEM127 knockdown restores mTOR signaling and proliferation.

claim: METTL3a is required for mTOR activation at least partially through m6A-mediated suppression of TMEM127 expression.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that METTL3a is required for mTOR activation at least partially through m6A-mediated suppression of TMEM127 expression, and this modulation contributes to tumor cell proliferation.
evidence: Conclusion based on m6A-seq, expression analysis, and rescue experiments.

claim: Proteasomal inhibitors MG132 and Ixazomib can largely block the generation of METTL3 short forms.
source: It is well known that proteolytic cleavage mediates post-translational process of protein into small pieces, to identify the potential protease responsible for this process, we screened a series of inhibitors targeting different proteases and found that the proteasomal inhibitors MG132 and Ixazomib could largely block the generation of these short forms (Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Protease inhibitor screen identifies proteasome inhibitors as blocking cleavage.

claim: Proteasome is a multi-catalytic protease complex that regulates cellular protein homeostasis through targeted degradation of proteins.
source: Proteasome is multi-catalytic protease complex that regulates cellular protein homeostasis through targeted degradation of proteins (Bochtler et al., 1999), and previous work has described the endoproteolytic activity underlying proteasomal function (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004; Liu et al., 2003; Sorokin et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Bochtler et al., 1999).

claim: Previous work has described the endoproteolytic activity underlying proteasomal function.
source: Proteasome is multi-catalytic protease complex that regulates cellular protein homeostasis through targeted degradation of proteins (Bochtler et al., 1999), and previous work has described the endoproteolytic activity underlying proteasomal function (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004; Liu et al., 2003; Sorokin et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004; Liu et al., 2003; Sorokin et al., 2005).

claim: MG132 treatment reduces the levels of both endogenous and exogenous short forms of METTL3 in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines.
source: Here, we validated that MG132 treatment could reduce the levels of both endogenous and exogenous short forms of METTL3 in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines (Figure 7b–d).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows MG132 reduces METTL3 short forms.

claim: MG132 inhibits the in vitro proteolytic cleavage of purified recombinant METTL3-His incubated with T47D cell lysates.
source: Further, MG132 could also inhibit the in vitro proteolytic cleavage of purified recombinant METTL3-His incubated with lysates of T47D cells (Figure 7e).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assay shows MG132 blocks METTL3 processing.

claim: Proteasome participates in METTL3 cleavage into the short forms.
source: These results suggest that proteasome participates in METTL3 cleavage into the short forms.
evidence: Conclusion based on proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: METTL3 interacts with the proteasome components PSMC3, PSMC5, and PSMD10.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays in 293T cells followed by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS)/MS showed that METTL3 interacted with the proteasome components PSMC3, PSMC5, and PSMD10 (Figure 7f), which was further confirmed by IP assays targeting METTL3-Flag in T47D cells (Figure 7g).
evidence: LC-MS/MS and co-immunoprecipitation identify proteasome subunit interactions.

claim: Knockdown of PSMC3, PSMC5, or PSMD10 abrogates the cleavage of METTL3 in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: In addition, knockdown of PSMC3, PSMC5, or PSMD10 abrogated the cleavage of METTL3 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7h–j).
evidence: Knockdown experiments show requirement of specific proteasome subunits for cleavage.

claim: 26S proteasome can directly cleave METTL3 WT to METTL3a and METTL3b.
source: Indeed, in vitro proteasomal cleavage assay by incubation of purified recombinant METTL3 with 26S proteasome showed that 26S proteasome could directly cleave METTL3 WT to METTL3a and METTL3b, while deletion of both L198 and Q238 inhibited this process (Figure 7k).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assay with purified 26S proteasome demonstrates direct cleavage activity.

claim: Deletion of both L198 and Q238 inhibits 26S proteasome-mediated cleavage of METTL3.
source: Indeed, in vitro proteasomal cleavage assay by incubation of purified recombinant METTL3 with 26S proteasome showed that 26S proteasome could directly cleave METTL3 WT to METTL3a and METTL3b, while deletion of both L198 and Q238 inhibited this process (Figure 7k).
evidence: In vitro cleavage assay shows mutant METTL3 is resistant to proteasomal cleavage.

claim: Proteasome is responsible for the cleavage of METTL3 into METTL3a and METTL3b.
source: These results support the hypothesis that proteasome is responsible for the cleavage of METTL3 into METTL3a and METTL3b.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including inhibitors, knockdown, and in vitro assays.

claim: mTORC1 promotes the expression of proteasomal subunits.
source: mTORC1 promotes the expression of proteasomal subunits (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: Silencing of mTOR in MDA-MB-231 cells inhibits the expression of PSMC3, PSMC5, and PSMD10.
source: Western blot analysis showed that silence of mTOR in MDA-MB-231 cells inhibited the expression of PSMC3, PSMC5, and PSMD10 (Figure 7l), and also led to decreased accumulation of the METTL3 short forms (Figure 7m).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows mTOR knockdown reduces proteasome subunit expression.

claim: Silencing of mTOR in MDA-MB-231 cells leads to decreased accumulation of METTL3 short forms.
source: Western blot analysis showed that silence of mTOR in MDA-MB-231 cells inhibited the expression of PSMC3, PSMC5, and PSMD10 (Figure 7l), and also led to decreased accumulation of the METTL3 short forms (Figure 7m).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows mTOR knockdown reduces METTL3 short forms.

claim: Treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines leads to decreased expression of METTL3 short forms.
source: Consistent with this finding, treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin in T47D and MDA-MB-231 cell lines led to decreased expression of these short forms (Figure 7n).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows rapamycin treatment reduces METTL3 short forms.

claim: Depletion of either Raptor or Rictor reduces the expression of METTL3 short forms.
source: In addition, depletion of either Raptor or Rictor, which are key components of mTOR complexes 1 and 2 (mTORC1 and mTORC2), respectively, also reduced the expression of the METTL3 short forms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows knockdown of mTOR complex components reduces METTL3 short forms.

claim: Raptor and Rictor are key components of mTOR complexes 1 and 2 (mTORC1 and mTORC2), respectively.
source: In addition, depletion of either Raptor or Rictor, which are key components of mTOR complexes 1 and 2 (mTORC1 and mTORC2), respectively, also reduced the expression of the METTL3 short forms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: Established knowledge about mTOR complex composition.

claim: Cells with constitutively active mTOR signaling due to KO of Tsc2 show upregulation of METTL3 short forms.
source: We also found that cells with constitutively active mTOR signaling due to KO of Tsc2, a negative regulator of mTOR activity (Crino et al., 2006), led to upregulation of these short forms, and proteasome inhibitor MG132 treatment could inhibit this upregulation (Figure 7o), suggesting that mTOR upregulates the METTL3 short forms via proteasome.
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Tsc2 KO cells shows increased METTL3 short forms.

claim: Tsc2 is a negative regulator of mTOR activity.
source: We also found that cells with constitutively active mTOR signaling due to KO of Tsc2, a negative regulator of mTOR activity (Crino et al., 2006), led to upregulation of these short forms, and proteasome inhibitor MG132 treatment could inhibit this upregulation (Figure 7o), suggesting that mTOR upregulates the METTL3 short forms via proteasome.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Crino et al., 2006).

claim: Proteasome inhibitor MG132 treatment inhibits the upregulation of METTL3 short forms in Tsc2 KO cells.
source: We also found that cells with constitutively active mTOR signaling due to KO of Tsc2, a negative regulator of mTOR activity (Crino et al., 2006), led to upregulation of these short forms, and proteasome inhibitor MG132 treatment could inhibit this upregulation (Figure 7o), suggesting that mTOR upregulates the METTL3 short forms via proteasome.
evidence: Immunoblot analysis shows MG132 blocks mTOR-induced METTL3 cleavage.

claim: mTOR upregulates the METTL3 short forms via proteasome.
source: We also found that cells with constitutively active mTOR signaling due to KO of Tsc2, a negative regulator of mTOR activity (Crino et al., 2006), led to upregulation of these short forms, and proteasome inhibitor MG132 treatment could inhibit this upregulation (Figure 7o), suggesting that mTOR upregulates the METTL3 short forms via proteasome.
evidence: Conclusion based on Tsc2 KO and MG132 treatment experiments.

claim: Proteasome is responsible for METTL3 cleavage, and the mTOR pathway positively regulates this process.
source: These cumulative results suggest that proteasome is responsible for METTL3 cleavage, and the mTOR pathway positively regulates this process.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experiments showing mTOR regulation of proteasome-mediated cleavage.

claim: METTL3a is essential for the METTL3–WTAP interaction and m6A deposition, resulting in the promotion of breast tumor progression.
source: In this study, we describe a cleaved form of METTL3, METTL3a, that is essential for the METTL3–WTAP interaction and m6A deposition, resulting in the promotion of breast tumor progression.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings from the study.

claim: The cleaved form METTL3a mediates the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, which is a prerequisite step for WTAP binding with METTL3.
source: Specifically, the cleaved form METTL3a mediates the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, which is a prerequisite step for WTAP binding with METTL3.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings from interaction studies.

claim: METTL3a is required for the global METTL3-mediated m6A modification and mTOR activation.
source: Analyses of the RNA m6A methylome reveal that METTL3a is required for the global METTL3-mediated m6A modification and mTOR activation.
evidence: Summary of m6A-seq and mTOR signaling findings.

claim: The mTOR pathway positively regulates the expression of proteasome components that mediate proteasomal cleavage of METTL3 into METTL3a.
source: Further, we find that the mTOR pathway positively regulates the expression of proteasome components that mediate proteasomal cleavage of METTL3 into METTL3a.
evidence: Summary of findings on mTOR regulation of proteasome-mediated cleavage.

claim: There is a positive feedback between METTL3a and the mTOR signaling pathway.
source: These findings reveal a positive feedback between METTL3a and the mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 7p).
evidence: Conclusion based on findings that METTL3a activates mTOR and mTOR promotes METTL3a generation.

claim: The core components of the MTC include heterodimers of the METTL3–METTL14 methyltransferases with an adaptor protein WTAP.
source: The MTC mediates m6A deposition. It is well established that the core components of the MTC include heterodimers of the METTL3–METTL14 methyltransferases with an adaptor protein WTAP.
evidence: Established knowledge about MTC composition.

claim: METTL3 undergoes METTL3–METTL3 interaction which is required for recruitment of WTAP in MTC.
source: Here, we found that METTL3 undergoes METTL3–METTL3 interaction which is required for recruitment of WTAP in MTC.
evidence: Summary of findings on METTL3 self-interaction and WTAP recruitment.

claim: Downregulation of METTL3a leads to decrease in both METTL3–METTL3 interaction and the METTL3–WTAP interaction, and consequently attenuates m6A modification.
source: Downregulation of METTL3a leads to decrease in both METTL3–METTL3 interaction and the METTL3–WTAP interaction, and consequently attenuates m6A modification.
evidence: Summary of findings on METTL3a requirement for complex assembly and m6A modification.

claim: METTL3a acts as a bridge between the METTL3–METTL14 heterodimers through mediating the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, thereby resulting in the formation of larger complexes which can efficiently recruit WTAP in MTC.
source: Based on this work, we propose that METTL3a acts as a bridge between the METTL3–METTL14 heterodimers through mediating the METTL3–METTL3 interaction, thereby resulting in the formation of larger complexes which can efficiently recruit WTAP in MTC.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: WTAP only interacts with METTL3 in dense phase.
source: In contrast to the constitutive binding of METTL14 to METTL3 in both the diffuse and the dense phase, WTAP only interacts with METTL3 in dense phase (Han et al., 2022), it means that WTAP tends to bind to larger METTL3–METTL14 complexes, which supports our conclusion.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Han et al., 2022) to support current findings.

claim: METTL14 binds constitutively to METTL3 in both the diffuse and the dense phase.
source: In contrast to the constitutive binding of METTL14 to METTL3 in both the diffuse and the dense phase, WTAP only interacts with METTL3 in dense phase (Han et al., 2022), it means that WTAP tends to bind to larger METTL3–METTL14 complexes, which supports our conclusion.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Han et al., 2022).

claim: The cleavage product METTL3a is a structurally appropriate component involved in MTC complex, whereas METTL3b is not.
source: It is also noteworthy that METTL3b contains the region of residues 239–580 but is not required for the METTL3–WTAP interaction. Based on our findings, we are inclined to speculate that the cleavage product METTL3a is a structurally appropriate (i.e., small enough) component involved in MTC complex, whereas the METTL3b is not.
evidence: Speculation based on differential functional requirements of METTL3a vs METTL3b.

claim: METTL3b cannot be further cleaved to produce METTL3a.
source: Besides, overexpression of METTL3b in T47D, MDA-MB-231, or 293T cells did not show METTL3a expression in these cells (Figure 3a, c, g), indicating that METTL3b cannot be further cleaved to produce METTL3a, and the METTL3 cleavage may require its N-terminal region.
evidence: Overexpression experiments show METTL3b does not generate METTL3a.

claim: METTL3 cleavage may require its N-terminal region.
source: Besides, overexpression of METTL3b in T47D, MDA-MB-231, or 293T cells did not show METTL3a expression in these cells (Figure 3a, c, g), indicating that METTL3b cannot be further cleaved to produce METTL3a, and the METTL3 cleavage may require its N-terminal region.
evidence: Inference based on observation that METTL3b (lacking N-terminus) cannot be cleaved to METTL3a.

claim: The proteasome exhibits endoproteolytic activity.
source: The proteasome is essential for degradation of intracellular proteins, including misfolded mutant and damaged proteins (Bochtler et al., 1999). In addition, proteasome also exhibits endoproteolytic activity (Liu et al., 2003), such as proteasome-mediated cleavage of translation initiation factors eIF4G and eIF3a differentially affects the assembly of ribosomal preinitiation complexes and thus inhibits the translation of viral RNA (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004), and proteasomal cleavage of the Y-box-binding protein 1 splits off the C-terminal fragment which can translocate into nucleus and participate in cellular adaptation to DNA damage stress (Sorokin et al., 2005), which are similar to METTL3 cleavage identified in this work.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Liu et al., 2003) and examples provided.

claim: Proteasome-mediated cleavage of translation initiation factors eIF4G and eIF3a differentially affects the assembly of ribosomal preinitiation complexes and inhibits the translation of viral RNA.
source: The proteasome is essential for degradation of intracellular proteins, including misfolded mutant and damaged proteins (Bochtler et al., 1999). In addition, proteasome also exhibits endoproteolytic activity (Liu et al., 2003), such as proteasome-mediated cleavage of translation initiation factors eIF4G and eIF3a differentially affects the assembly of ribosomal preinitiation complexes and thus inhibits the translation of viral RNA (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004), and proteasomal cleavage of the Y-box-binding protein 1 splits off the C-terminal fragment which can translocate into nucleus and participate in cellular adaptation to DNA damage stress (Sorokin et al., 2005), which are similar to METTL3 cleavage identified in this work.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004).

claim: Proteasomal cleavage of Y-box-binding protein 1 splits off the C-terminal fragment which can translocate into nucleus and participate in cellular adaptation to DNA damage stress.
source: The proteasome is essential for degradation of intracellular proteins, including misfolded mutant and damaged proteins (Bochtler et al., 1999). In addition, proteasome also exhibits endoproteolytic activity (Liu et al., 2003), such as proteasome-mediated cleavage of translation initiation factors eIF4G and eIF3a differentially affects the assembly of ribosomal preinitiation complexes and thus inhibits the translation of viral RNA (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004), and proteasomal cleavage of the Y-box-binding protein 1 splits off the C-terminal fragment which can translocate into nucleus and participate in cellular adaptation to DNA damage stress (Sorokin et al., 2005), which are similar to METTL3 cleavage identified in this work.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Sorokin et al., 2005).

claim: Deletion of METTL3 residues L198 or Q238 does not completely block the formation of their respective short forms.
source: Our data indicate that deletion of METTL3 residues L198 or Q238 does not completely block the formation of their respective short forms, leading us to speculate that the proteasome may recognize a conserved motif that likely contains multiple amino acids.
evidence: Observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The proteasome may recognize a conserved motif that likely contains multiple amino acids for METTL3 cleavage.
source: Our data indicate that deletion of METTL3 residues L198 or Q238 does not completely block the formation of their respective short forms, leading us to speculate that the proteasome may recognize a conserved motif that likely contains multiple amino acids.
evidence: Speculation based on incomplete blocking of cleavage by single residue deletions.

claim: The cleavage ratios between METTL3a and METTL3b are different among cell lines.
source: It is also noteworthy that the cleavage ratios between METTL3a and METTL3b are different among those cell lines. For example, the ratio of METTL3a to METTLb was greater than 1 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7c), less than 1 in T47D and 293T cell lines (Figure 7a, b), and equal to 1 in MEF cells (Figure 7o), we speculate that there may be some factors that control the cleavage ratio between METTL3a and METTL3b, which warrants further investigation.
evidence: Observation from immunoblot analysis across different cell lines.

claim: There may be factors that control the cleavage ratio between METTL3a and METTL3b.
source: It is also noteworthy that the cleavage ratios between METTL3a and METTL3b are different among those cell lines. For example, the ratio of METTL3a to METTLb was greater than 1 in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 7c), less than 1 in T47D and 293T cell lines (Figure 7a, b), and equal to 1 in MEF cells (Figure 7o), we speculate that there may be some factors that control the cleavage ratio between METTL3a and METTL3b, which warrants further investigation.
evidence: Speculation based on observed variation in cleavage ratios across cell lines.

claim: mTOR increases global m6A modification by promoting WTAP translation.
source: Other recent studies have demonstrated that mTOR increases global m6A modification by promoting WTAP translation (Cho et al., 2021), SAM synthesis (Villa et al., 2021), and by activating the chaperonin CCT complex (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Cho et al., 2021).

claim: mTOR increases global m6A modification by promoting SAM synthesis.
source: Other recent studies have demonstrated that mTOR increases global m6A modification by promoting WTAP translation (Cho et al., 2021), SAM synthesis (Villa et al., 2021), and by activating the chaperonin CCT complex (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Villa et al., 2021).

claim: mTOR increases global m6A modification by activating the chaperonin CCT complex.
source: Other recent studies have demonstrated that mTOR increases global m6A modification by promoting WTAP translation (Cho et al., 2021), SAM synthesis (Villa et al., 2021), and by activating the chaperonin CCT complex (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Tang et al., 2021).

claim: mTOR promotes the cleavage of METTL3 through positive regulation of proteasome components, thereby enhancing global m6A deposition.
source: Here, we reveal a new mechanism by which mTOR promotes the cleavage of METTL3 through positive regulation of proteasome components, thereby enhancing global m6A deposition.
evidence: Summary of novel mechanism discovered in this study.

claim: METTL3-mediated tumorigenesis largely relies on its methyltransferase activity.
source: METTL3-mediated tumorigenesis largely relies on its methyltransferase activity.
evidence: Established knowledge about METTL3 function in cancer.

claim: A selective inhibitor of METTL3 catalytic activity dramatically decreases tumor growth in mouse AML models.
source: The recent identification of a selective inhibitor of METTL3 catalytic activity that dramatically decreases tumor growth in mouse AML models suggests that m6A methylation by METTL3 could serve as a promising therapeutic target for cancer treatment (Yankova et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Yankova et al., 2021).

claim: m6A methylation by METTL3 could serve as a promising therapeutic target for cancer treatment.
source: The recent identification of a selective inhibitor of METTL3 catalytic activity that dramatically decreases tumor growth in mouse AML models suggests that m6A methylation by METTL3 could serve as a promising therapeutic target for cancer treatment (Yankova et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Yankova et al., 2021) and inference about therapeutic potential.

claim: The cleaved form METTL3a plays a key role in m6A methylation activity, providing a potential anti-cancer therapeutic approach through blockade of METTL3 cleavage.
source: Here, we show that the cleaved form METTL3a plays a key role in m6A methylation activity, thus providing another potential anti-cancer therapeutic approach through blockade of METTL3 cleavage.
evidence: Conclusion about therapeutic implications based on study findings.

claim: Proteasomal activity is upregulated in various cancers.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that proteasomal activity is upregulated in various cancers (Arlt et al., 2009; Chen and Madura, 2005), and several proteasome inhibitors have received regulatory approval and are routinely used in clinical settings (Manasanch and Orlowski, 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Arlt et al., 2009; Chen and Madura, 2005).

claim: Several proteasome inhibitors have received regulatory approval and are routinely used in clinical settings.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that proteasomal activity is upregulated in various cancers (Arlt et al., 2009; Chen and Madura, 2005), and several proteasome inhibitors have received regulatory approval and are routinely used in clinical settings (Manasanch and Orlowski, 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Manasanch and Orlowski, 2017).

claim: This study expands the rationale for targeting the mTOR–proteasome axis in breast cancer therapies.
source: Our study expands the rationale for targeting the mTOR–proteasome axis in breast cancer therapies.
evidence: Conclusion about therapeutic implications based on study findings.

claim: METTL3 activates mTOR, although the underlying mechanism has remained poorly defined.
source: Previous studies have reported that METTL3 activates mTOR (Chen et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020a), although the underlying mechanism has remained poorly defined.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Chen et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020a) with note about knowledge gap.

claim: The mTOR pathway is the most highly enriched signal transduction pathway affected by METTL3a depletion based on KEGG analysis of transcriptome-wide m6A sequencing data.
source: KEGG analysis of transcriptome-wide m6A sequencing data showed that the mTOR pathway is the most highly enriched signal transduction pathway affected by METTL3a depletion.
evidence: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of m6A-seq data.

claim: TMEM127 is the primary target of METTL3 among genes involved in the mTOR pathway.
source: Furthermore, we show that TMEM127 is the primary target of METTL3 among those genes involved in the mTOR pathway, and depletion of METTL3a decreases m6A modification of the TMEM127 3′UTR, leading to elevated TMEM127 expression.
evidence: Conclusion based on m6A-seq analysis and validation experiments.

claim: Depletion of METTL3a decreases m6A modification of the TMEM127 3′UTR, leading to elevated TMEM127 expression.
source: Furthermore, we show that TMEM127 is the primary target of METTL3 among those genes involved in the mTOR pathway, and depletion of METTL3a decreases m6A modification of the TMEM127 3′UTR, leading to elevated TMEM127 expression.
evidence: m6A-seq and expression analysis demonstrate mechanism of TMEM127 regulation.

claim: TMEM127 serves as a suppressor of the mTOR pathway by interfering with mTOR accessibility for its regulators.
source: TMEM127 serves as a suppressor of the mTOR pathway by interfering with mTOR accessibility for its regulators (Qin et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Qin et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2010).

claim: METTL3a functions as a positive regulatory feedback for activation of the mTOR pathway.
source: Thus, mechanistically, METTL3a functions as a positive regulatory feedback for activation of the mTOR pathway.
evidence: Conclusion based on findings that METTL3a suppresses TMEM127, which inhibits mTOR.

claim: This study represents the first description of cleaved forms of METTL3.
source: In summary, this study represents the first description to our knowledge of cleaved forms of METTL3, with METTL3a in particular serving as an essential component of the MTC complex, and elucidates the intracellular assembly process of the METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex.
evidence: Authors' claim of novelty.

claim: This study elucidates the intracellular assembly process of the METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex.
source: In summary, this study represents the first description to our knowledge of cleaved forms of METTL3, with METTL3a in particular serving as an essential component of the MTC complex, and elucidates the intracellular assembly process of the METTL3–METTL14–WTAP complex.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings about complex assembly.

claim: The positive regulatory feedback between METTL3a and the mTOR pathway may serve as the basis for development of therapeutic strategies for breast cancer.
source: These findings also uncover a positive regulatory feedback between METTL3a and the mTOR pathway which may serve as the basis for development of therapeutic strategies for breast cancer.
evidence: Conclusion about therapeutic implications based on study findings.
